content: 1. Health-care providers must not be required to report women seeking abortion-related care to law enforcement authorities. This ensures the protection of patient confidentiality and privacy, as emphasized by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health in their 2011 interim report to the UN General Assembly. 2. States must guarantee the availability of and access to confidential post-abortion care under all circumstances, as outlined in the Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 36 on the right to life (2018). 3. Women must have access to emergency medical care, including post-abortion care, without fear of criminal penalties or reprisals. This principle is supported by the Special Rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment in their 2013 report to the Human Rights Council. 4. Requiring doctors or health-care providers to report cases of abortion violates women's right to privacy, as stated in the Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 28 on gender equality (2000). 5. Measures regulating abortion must not violate women's and girls' right to life, jeopardize their lives, subject them to physical or mental suffering, discriminate against them, or arbitrarily interfere with their privacy. This is emphasized in the Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 36 on the right to life (2018). 6. Denial of therapeutic abortion can arbitrarily interfere with the right to privacy, as highlighted in the Human Rights Committee's decision in KL v. Peru (2005). 7. Requiring third-party authorization for abortion violates the right to privacy, as it imposes judicial intervention in decisions that should be resolved between a patient and their physician. This requirement has been shown to lead to unsafe, illegal abortions, as noted in the Human Rights Committee's decision in LMR v. Argentina (2011). 8. States should repeal and refrain from introducing measures that create barriers to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, including third-party or judicial authorization requirements for abortion. This is supported by the Committee on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights' General Comment No. 22 on the right to sexual and reproductive health (2016). 9. Criminalizing abortion is a violation of international human rights law (IHRL) and constitutes a form of gender-based violence that may amount to cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. States must repeal discriminatory provisions, including those criminalizing abortion, as emphasized in the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women's (CEDAW) General Recommendation No. 35 on gender-based violence (2017). 10. Forced or coerced abortion is considered cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. This includes cases involving women with disabilities, where such actions may constitute torture, even if conducted under lawful decision-making processes by a legal guardian, as noted by the Special Rapporteur on torture in their 2008 and 2013 reports. 11. Denial of abortion, health care, and bereavement support in cases of fatal fetal diagnosis causes suffering of sufficient intensity to violate the right to be free from torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. This was highlighted in the Human Rights Committee's decisions in Whelan v. Ireland (2017) and Mellet v. Ireland (2016). 12. Women, adolescents, and all individuals capable of becoming pregnant have the right to make informed, free, and responsible decisions about their reproduction, body, and sexual and reproductive health, free from discrimination, coercion, and violence. This right is rooted in bodily autonomy and self-determination, as emphasized by the Special Rapporteur on the right to health in their 2021 report. 13. Women with disabilities have the right to decide on the number and spacing of their children and to control matters of sexuality, including sexual and reproductive health, free from coercion, discrimination, and violence. This is supported by the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities' General Comment No. 3 on women and girls with disabilities (2016). 14. States must take steps to prevent forced abortion in conflict settings, as it violates the right to decide on the number and spacing of children. This is emphasized in CEDAW's General Recommendation No. 30 on women in conflict prevention and post-conflict situations (2013). 15. The right to information includes safe access to sexual and reproductive health information, including abortion-related information. States must ensure the availability of accurate abortion information and allow health-care providers to distribute it without fear of criminal sanctions, as highlighted in the Human Rights Committee's decisions in Whelan v. Ireland (2017) and Mellet v. Ireland (2016). 16. Health information must be provided in a manner consistent with individual needs, taking into account factors such as age, gender, language ability, education, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex status. This is emphasized in the Committee on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights' General Comment No. 22 on the right to sexual and reproductive health (2016).
